text: A popular open-air dance garden on the Boulevard du Montparnasse, haunt of students and grisettes in the 1820s and 30s. Courfeyrac's cure for Marius's gloom is the standard student one: go dancing.
quote: Here, come to the Chaumière.

text: Sceaux, a village a few miles south of Paris, held a famous Sunday dance in its park, reached by crowded carriages and carts. Grantaire's sneer that this is where 'all lost women' turn up reflects its reputation as a place of easy pleasure.
quote: the ball at Sceaux

text: Candlemas, 2 February, was folk weather-day: if the sun shone, the bear went back into its den for six more weeks of winter (the origin of Groundhog Day). Mathieu Laensberg was the supposed author of a cheap almanac from Liège, full of such sayings. Hugo uses the rhyme to date the snow that falls on the Gorbeau house.
quote: that ancient Candlemas day

text: Hapgood's English for a slang name for the police (in French, 'les cognes'). The girls on the boulevard use it, and Marius only half understands; it is the first taste in this part of the book of the underworld's own language.
quote: The bobbies have come.

text: Writing false petitions to the rich under invented identities was a recognised Paris trade. Each letter here plays to its reader: a Spanish royalist exile for a legitimist marquise, an abandoned mother for a countess, a playwright for a shopkeeper with literary pretensions, a 'dramatic artist' for a churchgoer. The spelling mistakes repeated across all four give the game away.
quote: all four were written by the same hand

text: After France crushed the Spanish liberals in 1823 and restored Ferdinand VII, Spanish exiles of both camps drifted through Paris and appealed to French royalists for help. 'Legitimacy' was the royalist watchword: the right of the old dynasty against usurpers. A sham 'Don Alvarès' is calculated to touch a marquise who mourns the fallen Bourbons.
quote: the sacred cause of legitimacy

text: Under the July Monarchy only men paying at least 200 francs a year in direct taxes could vote: fewer than 200,000 in a country of over thirty million. To sign oneself 'Elector' was a mark of solid bourgeois standing, which is why the letter-writer flatters a wholesale stocking merchant with it.
quote: Monsieur Pabourgeot, Elector

text: The Comédie-Française, the state theatre in the Rue de Richelieu, home of classical tragedy and comedy. Getting a play accepted there was the summit of a playwright's hopes; the begging 'man of letters' claims to have sent it a drama.
quote: the Théâtre-Français

text: A parish church in the Rue Saint-Jacques, on the slope of the Latin Quarter south of the Luxembourg. The 'benevolent gentleman' who hears mass there every day is the old man the begging letter targets.
quote: the church of Saint-Jacques-du-haut-Pas

text: Light comic plays with popular songs set to well-known tunes; their refrains circulated in the streets like hit songs. The girl hums scraps of them as she prowls Marius's room.
quote: she hummed scraps of vaudevilles

term: 'J'ai faim, mon père. Pas de fricot.'
text: A mock-cheerful street rhyme: 'I'm hungry, father. No stew. I'm cold, mother. No knitting.' The jaunty tune and the grim words together are the girl's whole manner.
quote: J’ai faim, mon père.

text: Slang names for a five-franc piece, the big silver coin. Five francs was several days' food for a family like this one, which is why the coin melts 'the avalanches of slang' in her head.
quote: Five francs! the shiner! a monarch!

text: A low chest of drawers, the one solid piece of furniture in Marius's garret. Standing on it brings his eye level with the gap near the ceiling.
quote: by mounting on the commode

text: Johann Kaspar Lavater, Swiss pastor whose books on physiognomy (1770s) claimed to read character in the face. Hugo borrows the idea for his portrait of Jondrette: vulture and pettifogger in one face.
quote: If Lavater had studied this visage

term: 'The Dream' and 'Maringo Austerlits Iena Wagramme Elot'
text: A cheap coloured print of Bonapartist sentiment: Napoleon in glory, and a sleeping child, Napoleon's son the King of Rome, whose crown a woman pushes away. The column lists Napoleon's victories, Marengo, Austerlitz, Jena, Wagram, Eylau, comically misspelled. The family who hang it call themselves 'fine Bonapartists'.
quote: Maringo Austerlits Iena Wagramme Elot

text: François Ducray-Duminil (Hugo spells him 'Duchray'), author of tearful, wildly popular sentimental novels around 1800. The volumes lying about the garret are the reading-room romances that also gave Jondrette's daughters their high-flown names.
quote: by Duchray Duminil 1814

text: French for rabble, scum. Hugo calls Jondrette's 'everybody is canaille!' a variant of Solomon's 'Vanity of vanities, all is vanity' (Ecclesiastes): the cynic's version of the preacher's despair.
quote: Canaille! canaille! everybody is canaille!

text: A hackney cab hired in the street, named after the Hôtel Saint-Fiacre where the first cab stand stood. Arriving in one marks a visitor as comfortably off; hence Jondrette's 'He is Rothschild', the name of the great banking family.
quote: He is coming in a fiacre.

term: 'I suppress the liberty of the press'
text: Jondrette's joke when his wife protests. Charles X's attempt to muzzle the press by decree was one of the July Ordinances of 1830 that brought down his throne; the phrase had become a catchword for tyranny.
quote: I suppress the liberty of the press.

text: François-Joseph Talma (died 1826) was the great tragic actor of the Empire, Napoleon's favourite; Mademoiselle Mars was the leading comic actress of the Comédie-Française. Jondrette, posing as the actor Fabantou, claims Talma as his teacher and Mars as his friend.
quote: I am a pupil of Talma!

text: Célimène and Elmire are heroines of Molière (The Misanthrope, Tartuffe), roles Mademoiselle Mars made famous; Belisarius was the Byzantine general said to have ended as a blind beggar. Jondrette casts himself as the ruined old soldier begging from the actress.
quote: Elmire would bestow alms on Bélisaire!

term: Cab tariff: two francs an hour
text: Paris cabs had fixed rates; by the hour, cheaper by the trip. Two francs was a day's pay for many workers. Marius, with sixteen sous in his pocket after giving away his five francs, cannot pay in advance, and the driver whistles and leaves.
quote: “Pay in advance,” said the coachman.

text: The tune of a comic song about Jacques de la Palice, whose verses state the absurdly obvious ('a quarter of an hour before his death, he was still alive'). The cabman's whistling is a mocking dismissal.
quote: the air of La Palisse

text: A prison in the Marais, in the old town house of the dukes of La Force, used from the Revolution for debtors and criminals awaiting trial. The 'Fosse-aux-Lions', the Lions' Den, was its yard for the most dangerous inmates.
quote: he was discussed at La Force in the Fosse-aux-Lions

text: The proverbially rich king of ancient Lydia. Jondrette's name for the old gentleman shows how he sees him: not as a benefactor but as a fortune walking into reach.
quote: The Croesus is caught

text: The poor of Paris heated and cooked with charcoal bought by the bushel and burned in a brazier, a portable iron pan. Two bushels for thirty sous is an odd extravagance in a household that has just doused its fire to look poor.
quote: “Two good ones.”

text: Latin: 'Alone with one alone, in a remote place, they will not be thought to be saying the Lord's Prayer', an old moralist's saying about suspicious meetings. Hugo uses it for the two men talking in the snow behind the wall.
Thieves' slang: 'balles' were francs. The man in the snow means the job is worth five hundred francs a head, against a risk of five to ten years.
quote: five hundred balls

text: One of the boulevard theatres on the Boulevard du Temple, the 'Boulevard of Crime', famous for melodrama full of murders and rescues. The two plotters chat about last night's melodrama while planning a real one.
quote: the Gaîté Theatre

text: Hapgood's rendering of 'coups-de-poing': small pocket pistols, short-barrelled and meant for close range, the kind a police officer could carry unseen.
quote: of the sort called “knock-me-downs.”

text: The house on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital is named after a former owner, which is why the inspector, holding Marius's key, mutters 'Former property of Gorbeau': he knows the building well.
quote: Former property of Gorbeau.

text: A heavy all-steel chisel for cutting metal, struck with a hammer; the name means it works on cold iron, without a forge. Jondrette hides the one he buys under his greatcoat.
quote: a huge cold chisel with a white wood handle

text: Charles X, last Bourbon king of France, reigned 1824–30 and was overthrown in the July Revolution. To dine like him is to dine like a king; by 1832 he is a king in exile.
quote: You shall dine like Charles the Tenth

term: 'Nos amours ont duré toute une semaine'
text: 'Our love lasted a whole week, but how short are the moments of happiness! Adoring each other for eight days, was it worth the trouble?' A sentimental song of the day the girl sings to Marius's mirror; the second, 'You leave me to go to glory', is another romance of parted lovers.
quote: Nos amours ont duré toute une semaine

text: Diogenes the Cynic was said to search Athens with a lantern for an honest man; Cartouche was the notorious Paris robber chief broken on the wheel in 1721. A thieves' dark-lantern is Diogenes's lamp put to the opposite use.
quote: worthy of Diogenes turned Cartouche

text: A gold coin of twenty francs, still called a louis after the old royal coins whatever king was on it. Four louis, eighty francs, is far more than the sixty the 'actor' asked for.
quote: He laid four louis on the table.

text: The popular name ('the Mire') for the Port-Royal maternity hospital and dispensary near the Gorbeau quarter, where the poor went for free treatment. Jondrette's story is that the elder girl has taken her sister there.
quote: taken her to the Bourbe

text: A Jacobin was a radical of the 1790s, and by extension any republican; a 'bousingot' was a young republican hothead of the early 1830s, known by his varnished sailor's hat. Jondrette protests he is neither, flattering his visitor's supposed respectability.
quote: I am not Jacobin, sir, I am not a bousingot.

text: The French gave presents (étrennes) on New Year's Day, and making the fancy cardboard boxes for sweets and gifts was a small trade open to poor girls. Jondrette claims he meant to apprentice his daughters to it.
quote: the making of boxes for New Year’s gifts

text: Gold twenty-franc pieces struck under Louis-Philippe, the king since 1830, nicknamed after him as earlier coins were called louis or napoleons. The four the visitor lays down are eighty francs, two years' rent for the garret, which lets for forty francs a year.
quote: the four miserable Philippes

text: Jacques-Louis David, the great painter of the Revolution and the Empire, died in exile at Brussels in 1825 after the Restoration banished the regicides. Claiming the daub is 'by David' is Thénardier's absurd attempt to put a price on a tavern signboard.
quote: painted by David at Bruqueselles

text: The men with blackened faces: Hugo calls them 'fumistes', stove-and-chimney workers, whose trade left them sooty. Soot was the cheap mask of the barrière bandit.
quote: the “chimney-builders,”

text: Cellini was the Renaissance goldsmith and sculptor; François Villon the fifteenth-century poet who was also a thief. Hugo's point: the galleys hold artists as fine as these, like the convict who can hollow out a sou to hide a watch-spring saw.
quote: There are Benvenuto Cellinis in the galleys

text: Frederick the Great of Prussia reviewed his drilled regiments at Potsdam with a famously cold and complete eye. Javert names each ruffian as he passes them in review, like a general who knows every soldier.
quote: a glance of a Frederick II at a Potsdam parade

text: Auvergnats, migrants from the poor mountains of central France, did much of Paris's heavy work as water-carriers, coal-heavers and porters, and had a name for settling things with their fists. The phrase means a rough-and-tumble brawl.
quote: collaring each other like men of Auvergne

text: Two Paris prisons for women. Saint-Lazare, an old leper-house in the Faubourg Saint-Denis, held prostitutes and women awaiting trial; the Madelonettes, a former convent for repentant women in the Marais, held others. With the father at La Force, the whole family is now behind bars.
quote: “At Saint-Lazare.”

text: A nonsense song, 'King Clog-chop went a-hunting, a-hunting for crows', sung by the gamin as he goes. It sets the tone of the scene: a child told where his whole family is jailed answers 'Ah!' and walks off singing.
quote: Le roi Coupdesabot

text: The 'Three Glorious Days', 27–29 July 1830, when Paris rose against Charles X, built barricades and drove the last Bourbon king into exile. It ended not in a republic but in a new king, Louis-Philippe. Hugo opens Volume IV with it because 1831–32, the years of this part of the story, are its aftershock.
quote: the Revolution of July

text: The two camps of the early July Monarchy: the 'Movement' wanted the 1830 revolution carried further, toward wider suffrage and support for liberal causes abroad; the 'Resistance' wanted it stopped and order kept. Hugo borrows the labels to describe the whole epoch.
quote: movement and resistance

text: A song by Béranger (1813) about a tiny, lazy, contented king who 'rose late, went to bed early' and made no wars. Hugo uses it for what a France exhausted by Napoleon wanted: a small, quiet king. Prusias, a minor king of Bithynia, plays the same role against Caesar.
quote: Napoleon for the King of Yvetot

text: The constitution Louis XVIII issued on his return, guaranteeing a parliament, equality before the law and press freedom. The Bourbons treated it as a gift 'granted' by the king, which he could take back. Hugo's point is that these were rights won, not favours.
quote: the charter of Louis XVIII

text: Four decrees signed by Charles X on 25 July 1830: they suspended press freedom, dissolved the newly elected Chamber, and cut the electorate to favour great landowners. Paris answered with barricades within two days.
quote: the ordinances of July

text: Hugo's English parallel. After Cromwell's Protectorate, Charles II was restored in 1660 and the Stuarts, like the Bourbons, overreached; James II was driven out in 1688 and replaced by a more pliable branch. France in 1830 repeated the pattern.
quote: what England demanded of the Stuarts after the Protector

text: Leaving France from Cherbourg in August 1830, the fallen king is said to have had a round table cut square on board ship so that court precedence could still be observed at meals. Hugo uses it to show the Bourbons minding etiquette while losing a crown.
quote: causing a round table to be cut over into a square table

text: A magistrate and moralist of the late sixteenth century. The 'day of the Barricades' he refers to was 12 May 1588, when Paris first barricaded its streets, against Henri III. His words of loyalty to fallen kings are what Hugo says France practised in 1830.
quote: Guillaume du Vair after the day of the Barricades

text: Agustín de Iturbide, a Mexican officer who had himself crowned Emperor of Mexico in 1822 and was overthrown within a year. Hugo's example of the 'first man of fortune' turned into a king, as against Napoleon, the man of genius.
quote: in the second, Iturbide

text: England's 'Glorious Revolution' of 1688 replaced James II with William and Mary, and later the crown passed to the German House of Hanover (Brunswick-Lüneburg). For Hugo, England had already shown how to halt a revolution by finding a new branch of royalty, which 1830 copied with the House of Orléans.
quote: the House of Brunswick or the House of Orleans

text: The middle class of property, trade and the professions, which ran France after 1830: only men of means could vote. Hugo refuses to call it a class or caste: 'The bourgeois is the man who now has time to sit down.'
quote: A chair is not a caste.

text: Louis-Philippe d'Orléans (1773–1850), head of the younger branch of the royal family, made 'King of the French' in August 1830. He styled himself a citizen-king: umbrella under his arm, sons at public schools. He is the king of this whole part of the novel.
quote: His name was Louis Philippe d’Orleans.

text: The 221 deputies who in March 1830 voted an address of no confidence in Charles X's ministry. When the king answered with the July Ordinances, the same Chamber offered the crown to Louis-Philippe. Hugo calls them a half-Parliament that elected a half-king.
quote: The 221 made Louis Philippe King.

term: Lafayette at the Hôtel de Ville
text: The Marquis de Lafayette, hero of the American and French Revolutions, commanded the National Guard in 1830. On 31 July he embraced Louis-Philippe on the balcony of the town hall wrapped in a tricolour flag, which won the crowd; the new regime was called 'the best of republics'. The town hall replaced Reims cathedral, where French kings had been crowned.
quote: Lafayette undertook the coronation.

text: The regime of 1830–48 under Louis-Philippe: a constitutional monarchy of property-owners, with a narrow electorate, the tricolour flag and a 'citizen king'. Hugo calls it 'the halt', a revolution stopped halfway; writing in the 1860s, he knows it lasted until the revolution of 1848.
quote: 1830 is a revolution arrested midway.

text: Louis-Philippe's father, the Duke of Orléans, who took the name 'Equality' in the Revolution and as a deputy voted for the death of his cousin Louis XVI, before going to the guillotine himself in 1793. Hence Hugo's 'a father to whom history will accord certain attenuating circumstances', and the jibe 'Prince Equality' at the son.
quote: To be Prince Equality

text: The first victories of the French revolutionary armies in 1792. The young Louis-Philippe, then Duke of Chartres, fought in both, which let the July King claim a revolutionary past.
quote: a general at Valmy; a soldier at Jemappes

text: Episodes of Louis-Philippe's foreign policy: French troops occupied Ancona in 1832 to check Austria in Italy; a French army besieged Antwerp in 1832 to secure Belgian independence; and in 1844 France paid compensation to George Pritchard, a British missionary expelled from Tahiti, to avoid war with England, which many French saw as humiliating.
quote: bombarding Antwerp, and paying off Pritchard

text: Louis-Philippe survived repeated assassination attempts. The worst was Fieschi's 'infernal machine', a rack of gun barrels fired at the king's procession on the Boulevard du Temple in July 1835, which killed eighteen people.
quote: attacked eight times by regicides and always smiling

text: During the Paris rising of April 1834, soldiers fired on from a house at 12 Rue Transnonain stormed it and killed the residents, men, women and children. Daumier's lithograph made it the emblem of the regime's repression.
quote: the Rue Transnonain

text: The 'pays légal': the small body of voters, fewer than 200,000 out of over thirty million, as against the 'pays réel', the real country. Hugo's 'three hundred thousand privileged persons' is the July Monarchy's whole electorate.
quote: the absorption of the real country by the legal country

text: Charges against the reign. Abd-el-Kader led Algerian resistance to the French conquest and was imprisoned despite a promise of free exile. The Duchesse de Berry, who tried to raise the west for her son in 1832, was betrayed for money by Simon Deutz and held in the fortress of Blaye.
quote: Abd-el-Kader, Blaye, Deutz bought

text: A wooden-and-iron cage in the abbey prison of Mont-Saint-Michel, said to date from Louis XI, in which state prisoners were confined. The young Louis-Philippe helped break it up in 1788, a gesture the liberal bourgeoisie remembered.
quote: the iron cage of Mont-Saint-Michel

text: Laws passed in September 1835 after the Fieschi attempt, which tightened press censorship and made it easier to convict for political offences. Hugo concedes they existed even as he calls Louis-Philippe 'a king of the broad daylight'.
quote: The laws of September are open to sight.

text: Banker and Louis-Philippe's chief minister from March 1831, the strong man of the 'Resistance', who crushed the Lyons rising and kept order at home. Hugo makes him stand for the narrow side of the bourgeoisie, against the king's liberal side.
quote: one of the victories of Casimir Périer

text: Louis-Philippe was overthrown in 1848 and died in England in 1850; Hugo wrote this chapter in exile on Guernsey, having refused to live under Napoleon III. So he writes of himself as a ghost testifying for another ghost: 'one shade may console another shade.'
quote: two tombs in exile

text: Supporters of the elder Bourbon line, who regarded Charles X and his grandson as the only lawful kings and Louis-Philippe as a usurper. With the republicans they attacked the July throne from the opposite side.
quote: the old legitimist parties

text: In 1832 a new word for thinkers such as Saint-Simon, Fourier and their followers, who turned from political rights to the organisation of work and wealth. Hugo sums their programme up as two problems: to produce wealth, and to share it.
quote: the generic title of socialists

text: Europe after 1830: no open war, but standing armies on alert and the great monarchies, led by Austria's chancellor Metternich, watching revolutionary France. Hugo calls it a 'ruinous expedient'.
quote: armed peace

text: Hugo's catalogue of the year: the last Prince de Condé found hanged (1830); Belgium's revolt against the Dutch Nassaus and its crown given to Leopold of Saxe-Coburg; Tsar Nicholas I crushing Poland (Warsaw fell in 1831); absolutist Ferdinand VII in Spain and Dom Miguel in Portugal; Austria in Bologna. At home, the banker Laffitte ruined, Benjamin Constant dead poor, Casimir Périer dead.
quote: the last Prince de Condé engulfed in the shadows

term: The cross torn from Notre Dame
text: In February 1831 a legitimist memorial mass at Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois set off a riot; crowds sacked the church and the archbishop's palace, and crosses were pulled from churches, Notre-Dame included. In the same mood the royal lilies were scraped off the king's carriages.
quote: the cross torn from Notre Dame

text: In November 1831 the silk-weavers (canuts) of Lyons, starving on falling piece-rates, rose under the banner 'Live working or die fighting' and held the city for days. Hugo calls it a servile war, a war of the labouring class, beside the political civil war in Paris.
quote: at Lyons servile war

term: The Duchesse de Berry in la Vendée
text: The widowed daughter-in-law of Charles X landed in the south in spring 1832 and tried to raise the royalist west for her son, the 'Henri V' of the legitimists. The rising failed within weeks.
quote: the Duchesse de Berry in la Vendée

text: Asiatic cholera reached Paris in March 1832 and killed some 18,000 people in six months, mostly the poor of crowded old quarters; Casimir Périer died of it in May. Rumours that the poor were being poisoned added to the anger in the faubourgs.
quote: cholera

text: The workers' district east of the Bastille, home of furniture-makers and artisans, which had stormed the Bastille in 1789 and risen again in 1830. Hugo calls it the 'powder-house of suffering and ideas', the place Paris watches whenever revolt is in the air.
quote: Paris kept an eye on the Faubourg Saint-Antoine

text: A Babouvist followed Gracchus Babeuf, executed in 1797 for plotting a communist 'Conspiracy of the Equals'. Henri Gisquet was Prefect of Police from 1831. The crowd suspects the loud 'Babouvist' on the corner post of being a police agent provocateur.
quote: beneath Babeuf, the people scented Gisquet

text: The great peasant rising of 1358 in northern France, named after 'Jacques Bonhomme', the nickname for a peasant. It came to mean any revolt of the poor against the rich. Hugo insists he does not use it as an insult: 'The Jacques were the poor.'
quote: The Jacques were the poor.

text: Ranks in the cell structure of the secret societies, borrowed from Roman army units of five, a hundred and ten men, with éclaireurs, scouts. The lists Hugo reproduces are from real police finds of 1832.
quote: quinturions, centurions, decurions, éclaireurs

term: The Society of the Rights of Man
text: The chief republican secret society of the early 1830s, grown out of the Friends of the People, organised in small sections with names like 'Robespierre' or 'Phrygian cap'. It dated its orders by the revolutionary calendar ('Pluviôse, Year 40') and was broken after the risings of 1834.
quote: the Society of the Rights of Man

text: Section names chosen to frighten: 'Ça ira' ('it'll be fine') was the revolutionary song of 1790 that promised to hang aristocrats from lamp-posts; 21 January 1793 was the day Louis XVI was guillotined.
quote: Ça Ira

text: The upper chamber of parliament sitting as a high court to try crimes against the state. It tried the rebels of these years in mass trials, and the defiant answers Hugo quotes come from its records.
quote: a man accused before the Court of Peers

text: A wine-shop game, a kind of skittles in which a weighted disc was rolled to knock down pins. It is a detail Hugo takes from the police reports.
quote: a Jeu de Siam

text: The Sibyl was the prophetess of ancient Italy who spoke in a frenzy; Ennius, an early Roman poet, gives the phrase. Hugo makes the faubourg's wine-shops into oracle-taverns where men grow drunk 'more on words than on wine'. 'Ingens', huge, is Virgil's word for the blind Cyclops.
quote: the “sibylline wine.”

text: The École Polytechnique, the military engineering school in the Latin Quarter. Its uniformed students were famously republican and had fought on the barricades of 1830, so Enjolras counts on them.
quote: you will see the polytechnic students

text: Guillaume Dupuytren, the most celebrated surgeon of the day, chief at the Hôtel-Dieu, whose clinical lectures drew medical students in crowds. Joly, the medical student, is sent to sound them.
quote: Dupuytren’s clinical lecture

term: The Barrière du Maine and Richefeu's
text: The barrier on the southern edge of Paris beyond Montparnasse, outside the toll wall, where wine was cheap; Richefeu's was a wine-shop there. Its marble-cutters and sculptors' workmen are the lukewarm recruits Grantaire offers to warm up.
quote: The Barrière du Maine

text: A waistcoat with wide lapels in the style of 1793, worn by young republicans of the 1830s as a political badge; Grantaire's is red. Prudhomme's revolutionary newspaper, Rousseau's Social Contract and the constitution of Year Two (1793) are the reading he boasts of.
quote: a Robespierre waistcoat

text: A follower of Jacques Hébert, the most violent and foul-mouthed of the Terror's journalists, guillotined by Robespierre in 1794. Grantaire calls himself 'a bit of a Hébertist' as a boast of being further left than the left.
quote: I am even a bit of a Hébertist.

text: A strong green wormwood spirit, then becoming fashionable in Paris. Enjolras tells Grantaire to sleep it off.
quote: Sleep yourself sober from your absinthe.

text: The south-west edge of Paris was honeycombed with old stone quarries, abandoned workings that made good secret meeting-places. The Cougourde's members in Paris meet in one.
quote: one of the abandoned quarries

text: A street of the old Marais quarter near the Hôtel de Ville, in the tangle of narrow streets where the risings of the 1830s were fought. Courfeyrac's move there 'for political reasons' is a radical student going where the fighting is likely to be.
quote: he had gone to live in the Rue de la Verrerie “for political reasons;”

text: Victor Escousse and Auguste Lebras, two very young poets who, after their play failed, suffocated themselves together with charcoal fumes in February 1832. Their suicide was much discussed as a symptom of romantic despair; Hugo cites them as a warning of where pure reverie can lead.
quote: Excess of reverie breeds men like Escousse and Lebras.

term: The Gobelins river and the Lark's meadow
text: The Bièvre, a small polluted stream that ran through the tanneries and dye-works of the Gobelins quarter to the Seine, here called the 'river of the Gobelins'. Near the Rue Croulebarbe it still crossed open meadows hung with washing. A passer-by gives one of them its local name, the Lark's meadow, and the word catches Marius.
quote: “It is the Lark’s meadow.”

term: Ulbach and the shepherdess of Ivry
text: A notorious crime of 1827: Honoré Ulbach, a young wine-shop servant, stabbed Aimée Millot, a young goat-girl from Ivry who had rejected him, and was guillotined; Hugo's passer-by places the murder in this very field. The passer-by's gruesome footnote is lost on Marius, who hears only 'Lark'.
quote: It was here that Ulbach killed the shepherdess of Ivry.

text: Two domes on the southern skyline of Paris seen from the Gobelins: the Val-de-Grâce, a seventeenth-century convent church turned military hospital, and the Pantheon, the former church of Sainte-Geneviève made into a temple to France's great men. The 'pole of the Deaf-Mutes' is the tower of the Institution for the Deaf in the Rue Saint-Jacques.
quote: the Pantheon, the pole of the Deaf-Mutes, the Val-de-Grâce

text: Némorin is the sighing young lover of Florian's pastoral romance Estelle et Némorin; Schinderhannes was a famous German robber chief executed in 1803. Montparnasse prefers playing the swain with the daughter to playing the brigand with the father, so he leads the girl off her post.
quote: preferring to play Nemorin with the daughter rather than Schinderhannes with the father

term: The Fosse-aux-Lions and the Charlemagne yard
text: Courtyards of La Force prison. The official name of the worst yard was the Court Saint-Bernard; the inmates called it the Lions' Ditch. Brujon is left loose in another yard, the Charlemagne, so the guards can watch whom he talks to.
quote: which the robbers called the Fosse-aux-Lions

text: Prison slang: a 'postilion' is a pellet of moulded bread with a note inside, flung over the roofs from one courtyard to another; to send it 'into Ireland' is to send it over England, from one land to another. Hugo glosses it himself; it is the first of many argot terms in this part.
quote: What prisoners call a “postilion”

text: Prison code: a ship's biscuit sent back about a proposed job meant 'nothing to be done here'. The girl sent to look over the Rue Plumet house returns one, and Brujon's scheme dies in a word.
quote: A biscuit, in the shady symbolism of prisons, signifies: Nothing to be done.

term: Delancre and the devils of Vauvert
text: Mabeuf's two treasured books on demonology. Pierre de Lancre was a seventeenth-century witch-hunting judge whose treatise on 'the inconstancy of demons' is a classic of the genre; the devils of Vauvert haunted a ruined château near the Luxembourg in Paris legend, hence the phrase 'au diable Vauvert', far away. 'Gobelins' is also an old word for goblins, which is why the old man half believes in a sprite of the Bièvre.
quote: De l’Inconstance des Démons

text: The blue dye, then imported from India and the Americas. Mabeuf hopes to grow indigo plants in Paris and make his fortune from 'balls of blueing', the washing-blue sold to laundresses; his experiments keep failing.
quote: The experiments on indigo had not been successful

text: A bitter dispute between two German jurists in the 1820s: Savigny, head of the 'historical school', held that law grows out of a people's history; Gans, a disciple of Hegel, defended reason and codification. Marius earns his bread translating such learned German into French.
quote: the Gans and Savigny controversy

text: A royalist daily newspaper of the Restoration and July Monarchy, read by old legitimists. Éponine's picture of 'barons' as old men reading it in the sun at the Luxembourg is not far from the truth.
quote: they read the Quotidienne for a sou

text: Washerwomen knelt on the banks of the Bièvre and beat linen with wooden paddles, one of the sounds of the quarter. Paris then had no piped water for most of the poor, and riverside washing-places were busy all day.
quote: the laundresses of the Gobelins beating their linen

term: The Rue Plumet and the Rue de Babylone
text: Two quiet streets of the Faubourg Saint-Germain near the Invalides, among the great town houses of the nobility. The Rue Plumet (today Rue Oudinot) was almost empty; the house's back lane comes out a long way off in the Rue de Babylone, so that its tenant can come and go unseen.
quote: the lane which ended in the Rue de Babylone

term: A chief justice in the Parliament
text: A 'président à mortier', one of the senior judges of the Parlement of Paris, the great law court of the old monarchy. Such men were expected to be grave; Hugo's magistrate builds a hidden love-nest for his mistress, a 'little house', as eighteenth-century fashion had it.
quote: a chief justice in the Parliament of Paris

text: The pavilion's styles: a steep 'mansard' roof after the architect François Mansart; interior decoration in the manner of Watteau, painter of graceful parties in parks; and rocaille, the shell-and-rock ornament of the rococo. Together they say: an eighteenth-century pleasure house.
quote: in the taste of Mansard

term: The Rue de l'Ouest and the Rue de l'Homme Armé
text: The two cheap lodgings kept as bolt-holes: the Rue de l'Ouest near the Luxembourg on the left bank, and the Rue de l'Homme-Armé ('the Armed Man') in the Marais on the right bank, far apart on purpose.
quote: the one in the Rue de l’Ouest, the other in the Rue de l’Homme Armé

text: 'Petites maisons': discreet villas on the edges of eighteenth-century Paris where noblemen and rich men kept mistresses and gave suppers. The grotto in the Rue Plumet garden belongs to that world.
quote: the epoch of follies and “Little Houses”

text: The citizen militia of Paris, revived in 1830 as the backbone of the July Monarchy. Every man who paid direct taxes, from about twenty to sixty, had to serve, buy his own uniform and mount guard several times a year; the shopkeeper in his bearskin became the symbol of the regime. Serving is the perfect disguise for a man who wants to look like any taxpayer.
quote: M. Fauchelevent, independent gentleman, belonged to the national guard

text: Marshal Georges Mouton, Comte de Lobau, a hero of Napoleon's wars, commanded the Paris National Guard from 1830. Disputing with him over exemption is what a man with nothing to hide would do.
quote: nor to quibble with Comte de Lobau

text: 'The month of flowers', April–May in the revolutionary calendar. Hugo uses the old republican name for spring as the abandoned garden comes to life.
quote: In Floréal this enormous thicket

text: The aristocratic quarter of the left bank, with the 'classic and splendid hotels' (town houses) of the Rue de Varenne, the Rue de Bourgogne and the Rue Saint-Dominique, and the dome of the Invalides close by. A wild garden there is a wilderness in the most formal part of Paris.
quote: the classic and splendid hotels of the Rue de Varennes

text: Horse-drawn public coaches with fixed routes and fares, new in Paris since 1828 and painted in company colours, yellow, brown, white or red. Hugo lists them among the city noises that fail to reach the garden.
quote: the yellow, brown, white, and red omnibuses

text: Paphos in Cyprus was the shrine of Venus, goddess of love. The magistrate's garden of gallantry becomes an Eden of innocence. Lamoignon was a great family of magistrates; Le Nôtre, the gardener of Versailles: the garden was laid out by a judge playing at one and a gardener playing at the other.
quote: Paphos had been made over into Eden.

text: White wheat bread was a mark of comfort; the poor ate coarse dark bread of rye or mixed grain. Cosette's protest at her father's 'horrible bread' is a protest at his self-imposed poverty.
quote: why do you eat horrible bread like that

text: The desert of the Thebaid in Upper Egypt, where the first Christian hermits lived. Hugo uses it for the hidden, solitary life in the Rue de Babylone.
quote: in that Thebaid of the Rue de Babylone

text: In songbooks allowed into the convent, the nuns replaced 'amour' (love) with 'tambour' (drum) or 'pandour' (a Croatian irregular soldier), which rhyme with it. The older girls puzzled over the nonsense that resulted. Cosette left too young even for that, so she has no word for what she feels.
quote: amour was replaced by tambour or pandour

text: General Louis-François Coutard commanded the Paris military division in the early 1830s. The sight of him in full uniform is what sets Jean Valjean dreaming of a gilded uniform of his own for Cosette's sake.
quote: Comte Coutard, the commandant of Paris

text: Until 1836, convicts sentenced to the galleys were sent from Bicêtre to the ports of Brest, Rochefort or Toulon by road in a 'chain': iron collars riveted on in the prison yard, then weeks on open carts, chained together, guarded by the 'argousins'. Its departures drew crowds. In 1836 it was replaced by closed cell-wagons.
quote: It was the chain-gang, in fact

text: Marc-Antoine Désaugiers was the most popular writer of comic songs and vaudevilles of the Restoration. The convicts bellow a medley of his on the road; Hugo sets the bawdy cheerful tune against the procession of the damned.
quote: a potpourri by Désaugiers, then famous, called “The Vestal;”

term: Fêtes on the Champ de Mars
text: Public holidays under the July Monarchy, notably the anniversary of July 1830 and the King's name-day, meant a review of troops and National Guard on the Champ de Mars, boat jousts on the Seine, free shows in the Champs-Élysées and fireworks at the Arc de Triomphe.
quote: a review in the Champ de Mars, jousts on the Seine

text: A sarcastic name for a vet, or a quack. Jean Valjean will not see a real doctor about his burned arm; a doctor's questions are the last thing he wants.
quote: “Call the dog-doctor,” said he.

text: The scrappy settlement of market gardens and cottages along the Seine beyond the Salpêtrière, named after the nearby Austerlitz bridge. It is where M. Mabeuf has his little house and garden, on the poor south-eastern edge of the city.
quote: the village of Austerlitz

text: Lancers were light cavalry armed with lances, with a plumed shapska helmet and spurs that rang on the pavement: the most showy uniform in the army. A cavalry barracks stood in the Rue de Babylone, so a handsome officer passing the gate every day was quite natural.
quote: the regiment in barracks in the Rue de Babylone

text: An opera by Carl Maria von Weber (1823), a German romantic tale of knights and wronged love; its hunters' chorus was famous. Hugo calls it 'probably the most beautiful thing in all the sphere of music', and lets its forest mood colour Cosette's fear of the dark garden.
quote: the chorus from Euryanthe

text: A marble copy of the ancient 'Borghese Gladiator' that stood in the Luxembourg garden. The young man's 'near the Gladiator' fixes the spot where their eyes first met.
quote: near the Gladiator

text: The covered galleries round the Odéon theatre, by the Luxembourg, where booksellers' stalls stood and students read the newspapers. A natural place for a poor law graduate to linger.
quote: under the arcade of the Odéon

text: The wife of a seventeenth-century Marshal of France, known (Hugo says) for loving her daughters and hating her sons. He uses her as precedent for a mother whose maternity stops at her girls.
quote: Like the Maréchale de La Mothe-Houdancourt

text: An old street off the Quai des Célestins in the Marais. Its name ('little musk', a corruption of an earthier medieval name) lets Hugo joke that Magnon could turn her bad 'odour' into good.
quote: this ancient street of the Petit-Musc

text: Croup, here meaning diphtheria, killed young children in waves along the crowded Seine quarters; doctors tried alum inhalations, later replaced by iodine. Writing in the 1860s, Hugo dates the epidemic 'thirty-five years ago', in the late 1820s.
quote: the great epidemic of croup

text: Rousseau, the philosopher of natural education, left all five of his children at the Paris Foundling Hospital, as he admitted in his Confessions. Thénardier's quip silences his wife's scruple about giving up her own boys.
quote: “Jean Jacques Rousseau did even better!”

text: Hapgood's English for a 'huissier', a bailiff or court officer who served writs and seized goods. M. Barge's address is on the paper the little boys lose.
quote: a retired tipstaff

term: The medals and Mademoiselle Mars's diamonds
text: Two celebrated thefts: in 1831 thieves stole ancient gold medals from the Royal Library's coin cabinet; in 1827 the jewels of the actress Mademoiselle Mars were stolen and partly recovered in a famous trial. Magnon's lodger, 'Mamselle Miss', is said to be mixed up in both.
quote: the medals in the Library and Mademoiselle Mar’s diamonds

text: Gavroche's name for his own sideline: smashing the windows of barbers' shops. The barber who has just thrown out two small children has earned his attention.
quote: “shaving barbers.”

text: Argot for the scaffold ('l'abbaye de Monte-à-Regret'): the steps one climbs unwillingly. Gavroche's joking answer to 'Do you know where I'm going?' is 'to the gallows'.
quote: “To the Abbey of Ascend-with-Regret,”

text: Paris street-talk. 'Kekçaa?' is 'Qu'est-ce que ça a?', 'What's wrong with that?', squashed into one word; Hugo calls it 'the language which no one writes, and which everyone speaks'. 'Tanflûte!' is a scornful exclamation, roughly 'Rubbish!'.
quote: Kekçaa signifies

term: 'Mon dogue, ma dague et ma digue'
text: Old slang of the Temple quarter, 'my dog, my knife and my wife', a showman's formula from the age of Molière and the engraver Callot. Montparnasse uses it to let Gavroche know, without saying so, that he cannot talk freely.
quote: mon dogue, ma dague et ma digue

text: Napoleon planned a colossal bronze elephant fountain, with a tower on its back, for the site of the Bastille. Only a full-size plaster-and-timber model was built, in 1814; it stood decaying in a corner of the square, full of rats, until 1846. Gavroche lives inside it.
quote: a singular monument

text: The bronze column on the Place de la Bastille honouring those killed in the July Revolution, begun in 1831 and finished in 1840. In 1832 it was still in its wooden scaffolding. Hugo calls it a 'stovepipe', and 'this monument of a revolution that miscarried'.
quote: the column of July

text: A patent tinder-lighter sold by a man named Fumade, a quick way to make a flame in the days before friction matches were common. Gavroche lights his candle-end with one.
quote: the Fumade steel represented progress

text: A gigantic wine barrel in Heidelberg castle, one of the sights of Europe, big enough to hold a dance on its top. Inside the elephant, the children feel as if they were in it, or in the whale with Jonah.
quote: the great tun of Heidelberg

text: The royal palace on the Seine, Louis-Philippe's residence. 'Do you want the Tuileries?' is Gavroche asking his guests whether they expect a palace.
quote: Do you want the Tuileries?

text: Frédérick Lemaître was the great actor of the boulevard melodrama, idol of the popular audience; the Ambigu-Comique was one of the boulevard theatres where such shows played. Gavroche's world of free amusements includes both, and the claque, paid applauders at the Opera.
quote: I’ll take you to see Frédérick Lemaître.

text: Sanson was the name of the hereditary family of Paris executioners; Henri Sanson held the post in 1832 and lived in the Rue des Marais. To Gavroche, watching the guillotine is one more free show.
quote: Monsieur Sanson.

text: Gavroche corrects the little boys' speech into street slang: not 'lodging' but 'crib' (piaule), not 'head' but 'nut' (tronche). It is his way of making them at home.
quote: you don’t say ‘lodgings,’ you say ‘crib.’

text: The ogre's cry in Perrault's Tom Thumb (Le Petit Poucet), 'I smell fresh meat!'. Hugo gives it to the rats of the elephant, swarming at the netting round the children.
quote: what the good storyteller Perrault calls “fresh meat,”

text: The top floor of the 'New Building' at La Force prison, called 'Fine-Air' with prison irony: a garret hall of iron-barred cells under the roof, used for solitary confinement. An old kitchen flue of the dukes' mansion runs up through every storey to it.
quote: a top story which was called the Bel-Air (Fine-Air)

text: Milton is the sublime poet of Paradise Lost; Arnaud Berquin wrote sweet little moral tales for children. A grim prison wall next to a flower-filled bathhouse yard is the sublime and the twee side by side.
quote: Milton viewed through Berquin

text: Antoine-François Desrues was a poisoner executed in 1777. The 'Endormeurs' were a gang who drugged their victims with doctored wine before robbing them. Thénardier drugs his guard the same way.
quote: the band of the Endormeurs, or “Sleep-compellers,”

text: Two slang words for 'ici', here: icigo from the barriers, icicaille from the Temple old-clothes market. Each tells the man on the wall who is speaking below, before he sees anyone.
quote: These two words, icigo and icicaille

text: Two famous robber chiefs of the eighteenth century. Their old-fashioned thieves' cant is to modern argot, Hugo says, what Racine's French is to André Chénier's: classic against new.
quote: spoken by Poulailler and Cartouche

text: In slang, to 'eat' a man is to kill or rob him. The narrator calls the remark 'frightfully transparent'.
quote: “Now, whom are we to eat?”

text: The secret slang of the Paris underworld: thieves, convicts, beggars and prowlers of the barriers. Hugo uses 'argot' and 'slang' interchangeably, and opens a three-chapter digression to defend writing it. For him it is not quaint jargon but 'the language of wretchedness', a tongue invented for war on society.
quote: It is the language of wretchedness.

text: Argot for the underworld as a whole, the tribe of thieves; 'la pègrenne', hunger. Hugo derives both from Latin 'pigritia', idleness, and builds a little genealogy: idleness the mother, theft the son, hunger the daughter.
quote: la pègre, for which read “theft,”

term: The Last Day of a Condemned Man
text: Hugo's own short novel of 1829 (he says 1828), the inner monologue of a man waiting for the guillotine, which included a thief who talks argot and caused an outcry. 'The narrator of this grave and sombre history' is Hugo speaking of himself.
quote: the author of The Last Day of a Condemned Man

text: The two novelists who followed Hugo in letting criminals speak their own language: Balzac in the stories of the master criminal Vautrin, Sue in The Mysteries of Paris (1842–43), a hugely popular serial about the Paris underworld.
quote: Balzac and Eugène Sue

term: The Hôtel Rambouillet and the Court of Miracles
text: The Marquise de Rambouillet's salon was the cradle of the précieuses, ladies of the seventeenth century who invented an affected refined language; the Court of Miracles was the beggars' enclave of old Paris, where cripples 'miraculously' stood up at night. Hugo puts them side by side: every class has its private language.
quote: The Hotel Rambouillet nearly adjoins the Cour des Miracles.

text: The Roman comic playwright Plautus wrote passages in Punic, the Phoenician tongue of Carthage, for a character in his Poenulus; they are among the few surviving texts of that language. Hugo's point: by writing down a despised speech, a writer may be the one who preserves it.
quote: Plautus rendered

text: Four great French admirals from the seventeenth century to Hugo's day. The language of the sea they spoke is, for Hugo, the heroic slang, 'to the fierce slang of the thieves what the lion is to the jackal'.
quote: Jean Bart, Duquesne, Suffren, and Duperré

text: 'But where are the snows of yesteryear?', the famous refrain of François Villon's Ballade of the Ladies of Bygone Times (1460s). Hugo claims 'antan', from Latin ante annum, 'the year before', as a word of beggars' slang that the poet-thief lifted into poetry.
quote: Mais où sont les neiges d’antan?

text: In the lore of old Paris the beggars and vagabonds were a mock kingdom with their own king (the 'roi de Thunes', or the 'grand Coësre') and their own language. A condemned 'king' scratched on a Bicêtre wall that kings of old always went to be 'anointed' at the Coësre's stone: the galleys.
quote: a king of Thunes condemned to the galleys

text: Louis Mandrin, a smuggler of the 1750s who fought pitched battles with the tax-farmers' men and was broken on the wheel at Valence; a folk hero. Hugo pairs him with Villon: argot was chewed by the bandit and spoken by the poet.
quote: it was chewed by Mandrin

text: Hugo digs argot like a geologist and finds layers from every language of the poor: Spanish ('gat', cat, from gato), Italian ('spade', sword, from spada), English ('raille', spy, from rascal), German ('caleur', waiter, from Kellner), Latin ('cadene', chain, from catena), Basque and Breton. Crowns are 'maltèses', after the coins used on the galleys of Malta.
quote: Do you want Spanish?

text: Samples of argot coined from nothing or by metaphor: 'le larbin', the lackey (a word that passed into ordinary French); 'le rabouin', the devil, later 'le boulanger', the baker who puts bread into the oven; 'la sorgue', night, and 'l'orgue', man, so that man is 'a derivative of the night'; 'la tronche', the head on the block, beside 'la sorbonne', the head that plots.
quote: the lackey, le larbin

text: Argot for 'it is raining': slanting lines of rain likened to the lances of the lansquenets, German mercenary pikemen of the sixteenth century. Hugo admires it as an old figure that 'bears its date about it'.
quote: il lansquine, it rains

text: The argot names for the police changed again and again as each became known: railles, roussins, rousses, 'dealers in stay-laces', coquers, cognes. The girls' 'bobbies' on the boulevard was one of these. Argot, Hugo says, flees understanding as its speakers flee the law.
quote: the police are railles, then roussins

text: Cartouche, the robber chief of the 1720s, and Pierre-François Lacenaire, the dandy murderer and poet guillotined in 1836, a celebrity of the July Monarchy. 'Cartouche's talk would have been Hebrew to Lacenaire': a century had changed the whole language.
quote: Cartouche’s talk would have been Hebrew to Lacenaire.

text: Argot words Hugo reads as moral lessons. The file that cuts a fetter is the 'bastringue', a dance hall, because free feet can dance; the dungeon is the 'castus', for its forced chastity; the convict is a 'fagot', firewood for hell; and the prison itself is 'the college'.
quote: he calls the saw the bastringue

text: Before the Revolution, men sentenced to the galleys waited in a cellar of the Grand-Châtelet prison below the level of the Seine, chained by the neck to a beam, unable to lie down, sometimes for months. Hugo says most of the galley songs, the 'lirlonfa', were born there.
quote: There existed at the Châtelet in Paris a large and long cellar.

text: Argot for informing on one's comrades: the informer feeds on a little of each man's flesh. For a community whose only bond is the secret, it is the worst crime.
quote: “to eat the bit.”

text: In argot a candle is a 'camoufle'; from 'seeing thirty-six candles' after a blow comes 'camouflet', a slap, which reached Voltaire's pen. Hugo's example of slang climbing 'from the cavern to the Academy'.
quote: Candle, camoufle.

text: In Greek myth the princess chained naked to a rock as an offering to a sea-monster, until Perseus came on the winged horse. Hugo ends the chapter with the human soul of the wretched as an Andromeda in the dark, waiting for a rescuer.
quote: a sombre Andromeda white and naked amid the shadows

text: Two kinds of refrain in prison songs: the 'maluré', a plaintive moan (malheur, misfortune), and the 'larifla', a jaunty nonsense chorus. Hugo dates the shift from the first to the second to the mid-eighteenth century, and reads it as the underworld losing its sense of guilt.
quote: The plaintive maluré was replaced by the larifla.

text: 'Pantin' was argot for Paris, and also means a jumping-jack puppet. Calling Louis XV 'the Marquis of Pantin' is the new mocking gaiety of the eighteenth-century underworld toward the king.
quote: “le Marquis de Pantin.”

text: The four 'sacred legions' of the eighteenth-century Enlightenment: Diderot's Encyclopédie, Turgot's economists, Voltaire, and Rousseau. Hugo absolves them, and blames the gutter writers 'patronised by a prince' whose books ended in the Secret Library, the locked collection of forbidden books.
quote: these are four sacred legions

text: Nicolas-Edme Restif (or Rétif) de La Bretonne, prolific author of the 1770s–90s, whose novels of Paris night life and sexual frankness shocked his age. Hugo names him as the writer who dug 'the most unhealthy gallery' among the masses.
quote: Restif de La Bretonne

text: Friedrich Schiller's first play (1781), in which a wronged nobleman becomes the chief of a band of outlaws in revolt against a corrupt society. Hugo takes it as the emblem of a moment when theft dressed itself up as protest.
quote: Schiller in his famous drama The Robbers

text: When the Tuileries were invaded in the February Revolution of 1848, the crown and its diamonds, including the Regent diamond, were carried to safety under escort of ragged men from the faubourg. Hugo uses it to argue that the Revolution had made a jacquerie impossible.
quote: By whom were the wagons containing the wealth of the Tuileries escorted in 1848?

term: The 14th of July and the 10th of August
text: The great 'days' of the Revolution: the storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789, and the storming of the Tuileries that overthrew the monarchy on 10 August 1792. On such days, Hugo says, 'there is no longer any populace': the crowd shoots thieves.
quote: a 14th of July, a 10th of August

term: Selling the field where Hannibal camped
text: When Hannibal was encamped before Rome, the Romans showed their confidence by selling the very field he occupied at full price. Hugo urges the same calm faith in progress against the fear of disaster.
quote: Let us sell the field on which Hannibal is encamped.

term: Two swans meeting on the Jungfrau
text: The Jungfrau is one of the highest peaks of the Swiss Alps, a byword for untouched snow. Hugo's image for two chaste lovers is two white birds meeting on a white summit.
quote: Two swans meeting on the Jungfrau.

term: The cholera in the lovers' May
text: The epidemic that reached Paris in March 1832 was still killing through the spring, with carts of coffins in the poor quarters. Hugo notes that the two lovers in the garden do not even notice it.
quote: They did not notice the cholera which decimated Paris

text: The refrain of a Béranger song, roughly 'Not so fast, my girl!'. Éponine mutters it to herself as she takes up her post by the loosened bar of the gate.
quote: “None of that, Lisette!”

term: 'Nous n'sommes pas le jour de l'an'
text: 'It isn't New Year's Day, for kissing papa and mamma': the masked ventriloquist's sneer at the girl who throws her arms round her father. New Year's was the day of family visits and embraces.
quote: Nous n’ sommes pas le jour de l’an

text: Thieves were notoriously superstitious. Brujon calls off the job because he has seen two sparrows fighting and jostled a quarrelling woman: bad signs. Hugo lets a superstition do what threats could not.
quote: this morning I came across two sparrows fighting

text: Argot: Pantin is Paris itself (also a village just outside it), so 'Where shall we sleep?' 'Under Pantin' means anywhere in town, or nowhere.
quote: “Under Pantin.”

text: Faublas, the young rake hero of Louvet de Couvray's eighteenth-century novel of seductions; Monsieur Prudhomme, Henry Monnier's caricature of the pompous bourgeois. Both kinds of men, Hugo says, deny that love has a soul.
quote: the Faublas and the Prudhommes add

text: Tyrants of legend and history: Busiris, the Egyptian king who sacrificed strangers; Tiberius, the suspicious Roman emperor; Henry VIII, who executed two of his wives. To Marius, a journey to England is a crime worse than theirs.
quote: no action of Busiris, of Tiberius, or of Henry VIII

text: Arnould Humblot-Conté, a pencil manufacturer and deputy, made a peer by Louis-Philippe. After 1830 the peerage was no longer hereditary and was opened to industrialists; seeing a pencil-maker in the House of Peers would once have outraged M. Gillenormand.
quote: M. Humblot-Conté, peer of France

text: Fighters of the 1830 revolution received a special decoration, the 'July Cross', and the storming of the Louvre on 29 July was one of the famous episodes. Bullets and cannonballs lodged in house walls were proudly labelled with the date. M. Gillenormand jeers at all of it.
quote: Are you one of those decorated by July?

text: Charles X's younger son, stabbed outside the Opera in 1820 by a man who wanted to end the Bourbon line. A chapel was planned on the spot; after 1830 it was abandoned, and the square became the site of the Louvois fountain. For an old royalist it is one more insult.
quote: the monument of M. le Duc de Berry

text: The extravagant dandies of the Directory (1795–99), with huge cravats, tight coats and mannered speech; the name mocks their habit of saying 'incroyable!' ('incredible!'). M. Gillenormand still dresses like one in 1832. Garat was a fashionable singer of that time.
quote: dressed, according to his wont, like an incroyable

text: M. Gillenormand confuses the Rue Plumet with the Rue Blomet, a street of his youth, and pictures barracks and pretty girls. Pamela, heroine of Richardson's novel, is the virtuous servant-girl courted by her master; for the old man, 'a Pamela in a garden' means a pretty mistress.
quote: In a garden, a Pamela.

text: The great parade ground in front of the École Militaire on the left bank, used for reviews and festivals, and empty on ordinary days. Its slopes are where Jean Valjean goes to sit alone and think.
quote: the most solitary slopes in the Champ-de-Mars

text: French subjects needed a passport issued by the authorities to travel inside France or abroad, with name, description and place of residence. For a man living under another name, getting one meant questions he could not safely answer.
quote: the difficulty of procuring a passport

text: Two accomplices of Fieschi in the 1835 'infernal machine' attempt on Louis-Philippe, both guillotined. Hugo names them as the kind of conspirator the police were hunting, any of whose nets might catch a man hiding a past.
quote: a man like Pépin or Morey

text: Jean-Maximilien Lamarque (1770–1832), one of Napoleon's generals, then a deputy of the opposition: a patriot who spoke for Poland and against the treaties of 1815, and popular with republicans and Bonapartists alike. He died of cholera on 1 June 1832; his funeral on 5 June was the chance the secret societies were waiting for.
quote: “Are you coming to General Lamarque’s funeral?”

text: Shakespeare's Othello is destroyed by jealousy; Voltaire's Candide is too innocent to suspect anyone. Marius, Hugo says, is a Candide in this: the lancer passing the garden never makes him jealous.
quote: That which overwhelmed Othello glides innocuous over Candide.

text: A short street in the old Halles quarter, between the Rue Saint-Denis and the market, named after the hemp-dealers (chanvriers) who once lived there. It disappeared in the rebuilding of Paris after 1850.
quote: the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie

text: The great printing houses of the Renaissance and after: Aldus Manutius in Venice ('in aedibus Manutianis', 'in the house of the Manutii'), the Estiennes in Paris, the Elzevirs in Holland. Their editions are a book-lover's treasures, and Mabeuf sells them one by one for bread.
quote: a Robert Estienne

text: A Greek writer of the third century AD whose Lives of the Eminent Philosophers is the chief source on ancient thinkers. Mabeuf's copy, printed at Lyons in 1644 with rare manuscript variants, is his last and greatest treasure.
quote: a Diogenes Laertius, printed at Lyons in 1644

text: The second-hand booksellers whose boxes lined the Seine embankments opposite the Louvre, and the shops of the Rue des Grès by the Sorbonne, were where scholars bought and sold old books for a few sous.
quote: under the Quai Malaquais

text: The old artillery arsenal and its library on the right bank, near the Bastille and the Austerlitz bridge. 'Fighting near the Arsenal' places the trouble where Lamarque's funeral procession was headed.
quote: “In the neighborhood of the Arsenal.”

text: The two friends of Molière's The Misanthrope: Alceste, who will not bend the truth for anyone, and Philinte, who makes polite allowances for everything. Hugo uses Philinte for the 'good sense' that always splits the difference.
quote: Philintus against Alcestis

text: The 'juste milieu', Louis-Philippe's own phrase for his policy: a middle way between reaction and revolution. Hugo mocks it as 'the lukewarm water party', the school that tallies what a riot costs and never asks what caused it.
quote: A whole political school called “the golden mean”

text: Jean Chouan led the royalist peasant guerrillas of the west in the 1790s, 'the war of thickets'; Jeanne was the leader of the republican barricade at Saint-Merry in June 1832, 'the war of the pavements'. Hugo pairs the two kinds of hero.
quote: the one has Jean Chouan, the other has a Jeanne

text: Hugo's own distinction, central to this part of the book. Insurrection is the whole people rising against a fraction that has usurped its rights, and it is in the right; revolt (or riot, uprising) is a fraction rising against the whole, and it is in the wrong. The same cannon is wrong at the Tuileries on 10 August 1792 and right in Bonaparte's hands in Vendémiaire 1795.
quote: the war of the whole against the fraction is insurrection

text: Two finance ministers of Louis XVI's era: the Abbé Terray, hated for arbitrary taxes and bankruptcies, and Turgot, the reformer who freed the grain trade and was met with riots in 1775, the 'Flour War'. The same fury, Hugo says, is just against one and absurd against the other.
quote: legitimate when directed against Terray and absurd when directed against Turgot

text: The 'gabelle', the royal salt tax, bred a whole population of smugglers (faux-sauniers) in the west who fought the king's men for generations. In 1793 many of them joined the royalist Chouan rising: rebels against the throne turned into its defenders.
quote: that long and bloody protest of dealers in contraband salt

text: Hugo's list of massacres he calls mere 'uprisings': Saint Bartholomew's Day (1572), the September Massacres (1792), the Glacière killings at Avignon, the Princesse de Lamballe torn apart by a mob, and Marshal Brune lynched at Avignon in 1815 by royalists. Miquelets, Verdets, Cadenettes and the Companions of Jehu were bands of the royalist White Terror in the south.
quote: the assassins of Brune, Miquelets, Verdets, Cadenettes

text: Prince Jules de Polignac was Charles X's chief minister and author of the July Ordinances; Camille Desmoulins was the journalist whose street speech set off the taking of the Bastille. Hugo's paradox: the minister was the rebel, the man in the street the lawful power.
quote: Polignac is a rioter; Camille Desmoulins is one of the governing powers.

text: From Juvenal's first Satire: 'facit indignatio versum', indignation makes the verse. Under the Caesars there could be no insurrection, Hugo says, so protest went into the satire of Juvenal, exiled to Syene in Egypt, and the Annals of Tacitus.
quote: The facit indignatio replaces the Gracchi.

text: Masaniello was the Neapolitan fishmonger who led a bread-and-tax riot against Spanish rule in 1647; Spartacus led the great slave rising against Rome. Riot is the stomach, insurrection the mind. 'Gaster' is the belly, from the Greek.
quote: Riot is Masaniello; insurrection, Spartacus.

text: A town in the Indre where, in the famine winter of 1847, hungry villagers attacked grain stores and killed a landowner; several were guillotined. Hugo's example of a riot that was right at bottom and wrong in form.
quote: Buzançais, for example

text: The vote for all adult men, introduced in France in 1848, after this story's time but before Hugo wrote it. He argues that once every man can vote, street insurrection loses its justification: 'by giving the vote to insurrection, it deprives it of its arms.'
quote: Universal suffrage has this admirable property

text: Hugo was in Paris in June 1832 and saw part of the fighting himself; in the next chapters he places 'the author of this book' under fire in the Passage du Saumon. He warns that he alters names but that the episode he tells is real.
quote: “We have seen this.”

text: On 5 June 1832 Lamarque's coffin was taken in procession from his house along the boulevards to the Austerlitz bridge, to be sent on to his native Landes. Ten thousand National Guards escorted it, followed by students, workers, secret societies and foreign exiles with Polish, Italian, German and Spanish flags, while the government kept troops ready all round.
quote: General Lamarque’s funeral procession traversed Paris

text: Maximilien Foy, another of Napoleon's generals, became the great liberal orator of the Restoration Chamber; his funeral in 1825 drew a hundred thousand mourners. Lamarque was his successor in both roles.
quote: Like Foy, his predecessor

text: 'In petto', in the breast, is used of cardinals the Pope has named secretly. Lamarque, Gérard and Drouet were the generals Napoleon would have made marshals had the Empire lasted.
quote: one of Napoleon’s marshals in petto

text: The paid, professional police troops of Paris created after 1830, foot and horse, distinct from the citizen National Guard and from the army. They were hated in the working quarters as the regime's street enforcers, and they were the first sent in against barricades.
quote: the Municipal Guard echelonned from street to street

text: Today's Place de la Concorde, where Louis XVI was guillotined. Its name changed with every regime (Louis XV, Revolution, Concord); in 1832 cavalry with loaded muskets waited there during the funeral.
quote: the Place Louis XV

text: Napoleon's only legitimate son, once King of Rome, brought up in Austria under this title. Bonapartists dreamed of him as Napoleon II; in June 1832 he was dying of tuberculosis in Vienna, aged twenty-one.
quote: the Duc de Reichstadt

text: The bronze column in the Place Vendôme cast from cannon captured at Austerlitz, with Napoleon on top. Carrying the old soldier's coffin round it was a Bonapartist homage.
quote: the coffin borne round the Vendome column

text: The cockerel was the emblem the July Monarchy put on its flags in place of the Bourbon lilies and the Napoleonic eagle. Tearing it off a banner and dragging it in the mud was an insult to the regime.
quote: the Gallic cock torn from a popular flag

term: The red flag at the Austerlitz bridge
text: During Lafayette's farewell speech a man in black on horseback appeared with a red flag, or a pike capped with a red liberty-cap. Red was the colour of the most radical republicans; Lafayette turned away, and General Exelmans left the procession. Within minutes shots were fired and the riot began.
quote: a man on horseback, clad in black, made his appearance in the middle of the group with a red flag

text: The Pantheon was where the nation buried its great men; the Town-hall, the Hôtel de Ville, was where Lafayette had launched Louis-Philippe in 1830. The crowd's two shouts meant: honour the hero as the Revolution would, and start 1830 over again.
quote: “Lamarque to the Pantheon!—Lafayette to the Town-hall!”

text: Dragoons were mounted troops who could fight on horse or foot; carabineers were heavy cavalry in steel breastplates. Both were held ready around the procession, the dragoons in the Célestins barracks by the river.
quote: the dragoons emerged from the Célestins

text: A small island in the Seine near the Arsenal, joined to the right bank in 1843 when the channel was filled in. In 1832 it was a vast timber-yard, and its stacks of wood made a ready-made fortress.
quote: the timber-yards of the Isle Louviers

text: The heart of the June rising: around the church of Saint-Merry in the Rue Saint-Martin, insurgents led by Charles Jeanne made house No. 50 and the barricades on either side of it their fortress. It became the best-known stronghold of the June days, and its tocsin is the sound of this part of the book.
quote: that famous house No. 50, which was the fortress of Jeanne and her six hundred companions

text: The old central market district of Paris, between the Rue Saint-Denis and the Rue Saint-Martin: a maze of narrow, crooked medieval streets 'more intricate than a forest', perfect for barricades. Twenty-seven rose there in under an hour.
quote: twenty-seven barricades sprang out of the earth in the quarter of the Halles alone

text: A type of light horse-drawn public coach, one of the omnibus lines' vehicles. Overturned, any big carriage made the backbone of a barricade.
quote: made with an “écossais,”

text: A covered shopping arcade off the Rue Montmartre. Hugo tells us that he himself, 'an observer, a dreamer, the author of this book', was trapped there between the two fires for half an hour on the evening of 5 June.
quote: the Passage du Saumon became the field of battle

text: The commanders against the rising: Marshal Lobau, head of the Paris National Guard; General Bugeaud, a hard soldier later blamed for the Rue Transnonain and notorious in Algeria; and Marshal Soult, Minister of War, a veteran of Austerlitz, who hesitated that evening.
quote: Two intrepid men, tried in great wars, the Marshal Lobau and General Bugeaud

text: In July 1830 the 53rd infantry regiment refused to fire on the people and was cheered by the crowds. In June 1832 everyone remembered it, and no one was sure the soldiers would shoot.
quote: the neutrality of the 53rd of the Line in July, 1830

text: The alarm bell, rung fast and without stopping to call people out in fire, war or revolt. The insurgents rang the bell of Saint-Merry all through the night of 5 June, and all Paris heard it.
quote: the Saint-Merry tocsin began to make itself heard

text: The rising of the Society of the Seasons led by Barbès and Blanqui on 12 May 1839, fought in the same Rue Saint-Martin quarter and crushed in a day. Hugo cites it for the old cocoa-seller serving both sides.
quote: At the time of the insurrection of 1839

text: Carrel was the editor of the liberal paper Le National, the leading opposition journalist; Clausel, a Napoleonic marshal. The rumour that Carrel asked Clausel to lead the rising and was told 'Get a regiment first' is among the stories flying round frightened Paris.
quote: Armand Carrel had been to see Marshal Clausel

text: Ann Radcliffe, the English novelist of Gothic terror (The Mysteries of Udolpho). Hugo jokes that the police's lurid rumours of night pillage sound like one of her novels.
quote: that Anne Radcliffe mixed up with the Government

term: The 'Rue de Paris' of the Conciergerie
text: The long vaulted hall of the medieval Conciergerie prison, nicknamed the Rue de Paris. On the night of 5 June it was strewn with straw and packed with arrested men, among them Lagrange, a leader of the Lyons rising.
quote: the long vault which is called the Rue de Paris

text: A big horse-pistol, made to be carried in a holster on the saddle. The one Gavroche 'borrows' from a junk shop in the Rue Ménilmontant turns out to have no trigger.
quote: an old holster-pistol

text: A hill village of vineyards and cheap open-air taverns just outside the north-east wall of Paris, where working people went on Sundays. Gavroche comes down from it with a branch of laburnum.
quote: on the heights of Belleville

text: Pierre Baour-Lormian, a now-forgotten poet and translator of Ossian, member of the French Academy, whose members are 'the Forty' (immortals). Gavroche once ran an errand for him, which makes him, Hugo jokes, 'a gamin of letters'.
quote: M. Baour-Lormian, one of the Forty

text: The old aristocratic quarter of the right bank between the Hôtel de Ville and the Bastille, full of seventeenth-century town houses gone shabby, and quiet old people. Hugo contrasts its sleepy apathy with the uproar around it.
quote: This apathy, peculiar to the Marais

text: The witches' prophecy to Macbeth on the heath in Shakespeare. Hugo says three old crones of a Paris crossroads could have greeted Bonaparte with it as well as any weird sisters.
quote: the “Thou shalt be King” could be quite as mournfully hurled at Bonaparte

term: The King of Rome and the Duc de Bordeaux
text: The gossips' royal nostalgia: Napoleon's baby son, the King of Rome, who was driven round the Tuileries in a little carriage drawn by sheep; and the Duc de Bordeaux, Charles X's grandson, the 'miracle child' born after his father's murder in 1820, now in exile.
quote: the little carriage of the King of Rome

text: The 'chiffonnier', who walked the streets at night with basket and hook, picking rags, bones and paper out of the rubbish to sell. They were the lowest recognised trade in Paris, and proud of it: 'I have a profession.'
quote: the ragpicker interposed

text: The square before the church of Saint-Gervais behind the Hôtel de Ville, named after an ancient elm under which, by tradition, justice was done and debts paid. Gavroche is heading back into the riot's centre.
quote: l’Orme-Saint-Gervais

text: The old soldier's wounds read like a list of Napoleon's battles: Marengo, Austerlitz, Jena, Friedland, the Moskowa (Borodino), Lützen, Waterloo. A 'biscaïen' was a heavy musket-ball or grapeshot. Napoleon was wounded once, in the foot, at Ratisbon in 1809.
quote: a ball from a biscaïen in the thigh

term: 'Dialogue between the razor and the sword'
text: Hugo imagines Monsieur Prudhomme, Henry Monnier's pompous bourgeois, giving the barber's talk a grand title. The shopkeeper wishing for a hero's cannonball, and the soldier's dry answer, are the comedy of the scene.
quote: “Dialogue between the razor and the sword.”

text: A small market square behind the Hôtel de Ville, with a guard-post the insurgents disarm. It is where the students' band forms up.
quote: in the Marché Saint-Jean, where the post had already been disarmed

text: Poland's rising against Russia had been crushed in 1831, and Polish exiles filled Paris; their cause was a passion of French republicans and of General Lamarque himself. The students shout for it as they march.
quote: “Long live Poland!”

text: Each year the Archbishop of Paris posted a pastoral letter setting the rules for Lent, including permission to eat eggs on fast days. The archbishop in 1832 was the legitimist de Quélen, much hated since the sack of his palace; Bahorel tears his notice down.
quote: a permission to eat eggs, a Lenten admonition addressed by the Archbishop of Paris

text: Latin. 'Hercle!' is 'by Hercules!', a Roman oath, which Bahorel glosses with student cheek as 'cursed name of a dog'. 'Para bellum', 'prepare for war', from the proverb 'if you want peace, prepare for war'. Gavroche feels he now understands Latin.
quote: “What does Hercle mean?”

text: Gavroche's street contraction of 'Qu'est-ce que c'est que ça?', 'What's that?'. He asks it about the very old man marching with the band.
quote: “Keksekça?” said he to Courfeyrac.

text: A member of the revolutionary Convention who had voted in 1793 for the death of Louis XVI. To young republicans of 1832 such survivors were living relics of the great Revolution, which is why the rumour runs through the column about the old man.
quote: a former member of the Convention—an old regicide

text: Villages round Paris, rhymed for nonsense in Gavroche's song: 'Tou tou tou, for Chatou'. The song itself is about two drunken sparrows who have drunk the dew off the thyme.
quote: Pour Chatou.

text: The particle 'de' marks a noble name. Courfeyrac, a republican, will not be called 'Monsieur de Courfeyrac' and threatens to make the concierge 'Mother de Veuvain' in revenge.
quote: if you call me Monsieur de Courfeyrac again

text: The porter or portress who lived in a lodge by the street door of a Paris house, took in letters, watched comings and goings and knew everyone's business. Hapgood uses 'portress' and 'concierge' for the same job.
quote: I’m the concierge

text: A broad new street driven through the old Halles quarter in the late 1830s by the Prefect Rambuteau, the first of the great clearances of medieval Paris. It swallowed the Rue de la Chanvrerie and Corinthe; Hugo writes as one describing a vanished city.
quote: The Rue de la Chanvrerie and Corinthe have disappeared beneath the pavement of the Rue Rambuteau.

text: To map the spot Hugo uses the device he used for Waterloo: a letter. Picture an N with its top on the Rue Saint-Denis and its foot on the Halles: its two uprights are the Rue de la Grande-Truanderie and the Rue de la Chanvrerie, its crossbar the Rue de la Petite-Truanderie, and the crooked Rue Mondétour slices across all three.
quote: the simple means which we have already employed in the case of Waterloo

text: Street names of the old Halles: the Rue Mondétour ('my detour') and the Rue Pirouette, whose very names, Hugo says, describe their windings. The Pointe Saint-Eustache, by the great market church, was the corner they led to.
quote: The name of Mondétour paints marvellously well the sinuosities of that whole set of streets.

text: Two poets of the early seventeenth century who drank in this quarter: Théophile de Viau, whose couplet describes the skeleton of a hanged lover swinging there, and the satirist Mathurin Régnier, who drank at the wine-shop when it was still the Pot-aux-Roses.
quote: old Theophilus described in the following couplet

text: The wine-shop's old name, painted as a rebus: a post (poteau) coloured rose. 'Découvrir le pot aux roses' is also an idiom for uncovering a secret.
quote: this cabaret was called the Pot-aux-Roses

text: The wine-shop at the corner of the Rue de la Chanvrerie, renamed after a bunch of Corinth grapes ('Au Raisin de Corinthe') that the painter Natoire, a regular, painted on its post. It became the A.B.C. students' second meeting-place.
quote: “Au Raisin de Corinthe.” Hence the name of Corinthe.

text: Hucheloup painted 'CARPES AU GRAS' ('carps cooked with meat', his speciality) on his wall; rain washed away letters and left 'Carpe horas', Latin for 'seize the hours', as in Horace's 'carpe diem'. The cook who knew no French had written a motto.
quote: Carpe ho ras

text: The nicknames of Corinthe's two serving-maids. A matelote is a fish stew in wine, a gibelotte a rabbit stew: the students named them after dishes on the menu.
quote: Two serving-maids, named Matelote and Gibelotte

term: 'Régale si tu peux et mange si tu l'oses'
text: Courfeyrac's chalked motto on the door: 'Treat if you can, and eat if you dare', a parody of a line of classical verse. A fair warning about Corinthe's kitchen.
quote: Régale si tu peux et mange si tu l’oses.
