text: Three antiquarian historians of Paris from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, who catalogued its churches and convents. Grantaire cites them on the swarms of monks, Franciscans, Minims, Capuchins, Augustines, who once filled the quarter.
quote: Du Breul and Sauval give a list of them, and so does the Abbé Lebeuf.

text: In Livy, the Gauls under Brennus attacked the Etruscan town of Clusium; Rome protested, and the Gauls answered that Rome had done the same to Alba and Fidenae, then sacked Rome itself. Grantaire's drunken lesson: every conquest is a theft.
quote: Brennus took Rome.

text: The Great Comet of 1811, visible for months, was taken as an omen of Napoleon's war with Russia. Grantaire calls history a poster with 'the comet of 1811 at the head': heaven itself puts on a show.
quote: the comet of 1811 at the head of the poster

text: Joly, the medical student and hypochondriac, has a head cold, so his m's and n's come out as b's and d's: 'Barius' for Marius, 'dod't' for don't, 'abberent' for apparent. Hugo spells it out.
quote: it is decidedly abberent that Barius is in love

text: Hugo lists the names of errand-boys by trade: the baker's lad is a 'mitron' (for his paper cap), the notary's a 'saute-ruisseau' (skip-the-gutter), the cook's a scullion, the sailor's a cabin-boy. The boy who brings a message from Enjolras is little Navet.
quote: the baker’s gamin is called a mitron

text: Charles X's last minister, imprisoned since 1830. Navet's being 'the one to shout Down with Polignac' is a child's bit of borrowed politics, two years out of date.
quote: I’m the one to shout ‘Down with Polignac!’

text: Paris had barricaded its streets since 1588, and in 1830 and 1832 the method was well known: tear up the paving-stones (big sandstone cubes laid in sand) with bars and picks, overturn the heaviest vehicle at hand, and pile casks, furniture and stones round it. Here a lime-dealer's dray, the widow's casks and a hijacked omnibus make the core; the whole is done in under an hour.
quote: the dray of a lime-dealer named Anceau

text: Bossuet's pun as he stops an omnibus: the Latin proverb 'Not everyone may go to Corinth' (because pleasure there was costly), where 'omnibus' means 'to everyone'. Here it means: omnibuses do not get past the Corinthe.
quote: Non licet omnibus adire Corinthum.

text: Pygmalion, the sculptor in Ovid who fell in love with his statue and prayed Venus to bring it to life. Grantaire's version: a medieval mason fell in love with his ugliest gargoyle, and the result was Matelote.
quote: a Gothic Pygmalion

text: Leonidas and his three hundred Spartans died holding the pass of Thermopylae against Persia; Cromwell's Puritan army stormed Drogheda in Ireland in 1649 and burned defenders in a church steeple. Enjolras, Spartan and Puritan, would have fought at either.
quote: He would have perished at Thermopylae with Leonidas

text: The police fined householders for anything that fell or was hung out of a window into the street. Mother Hucheloup still smarts at paying a hundred francs over a counterpane and a flowerpot, so Courfeyrac tells her the barricade is her revenge on the government.
quote: the government collected a fine of a hundred francs

text: 'Charpie': threads picked from old linen, used as dressing to pack wounds before cotton wool came in. Making lint was what women did on the eve of a battle; here the widow and her maids tear up dishcloths for it.
quote: tearing up old dishcloths and making lint

text: Louis-Philippe's name-day, Saint Philip's day on 1 May, was the July Monarchy's great holiday, with illuminations. Its leftover fire-pots and carnival torches now light the barricade; they are said to come from the grocer Pépin of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine.
quote: a basket filled with fire-pots, “left over from the King’s festival.”

text: Paris streets were lit by oil lanterns hung on ropes across the roadway. Insurgents broke them first, to darken the approaches and leave the troops blind; here every lantern in the surrounding streets goes.
quote: They smashed the only street lantern in the Rue de la Chanvrerie

text: Insurgents had guns but few cartridges, so they melted lead, pewter or brass and poured it into bullet-moulds, then rolled the balls with powder in paper cartridges. At Corinthe the kitchen fire melts down the widow's mugs, spoons and forks.
quote: moulding into bullets, pewter mugs, spoons, forks

text: A proverbial catch-all mixture from an old comic sketch, 'Madame Gibou's tea' in which everything is thrown into the pot. Gavroche's recipe for a barricade: put everything in.
quote: A barricade is Mother Gibou’s tea.

text: A redoubt is a small closed fortification. Two barricades at a right angle, the high one across the Rue de la Chanvrerie and the low one across the Rue Mondétour, with the wine-shop at the corner, make one; steps of paving-stones inside let the defenders climb up to fire, a gap at one end lets a man out, and the Rue des Prêcheurs is left open as a line of retreat.
quote: The two barricades united formed a veritable redoubt.

text: Jean-Charles de Folard, an eighteenth-century soldier and writer on tactics, whose jargon Hugo borrows for the open line of retreat: a 'branch' of the works.
quote: what Folard in his strategical style would have termed a branch

text: The tall fur caps of grenadiers, worn by the élite companies of the National Guard and the line. 'Not a single bearskin cap or a single bayonet' means no troops at all.
quote: without this handful of bold men seeing a single bearskin cap

text: A cartridge was a twist of paper holding a measured charge of powder and a ball, bitten open and rammed down a musket barrel. Thirty each, from Courfeyrac's coffer, is a soldier's allowance for a day's fighting.
quote: Each one received thirty cartridges.

text: Jacques-Antoine Manuel and General Foy, the great liberal orators of the Restoration Chamber. In 1823 Manuel was expelled from the Chamber by force. Prouvaire's poem dates his young love by them: 'Manuel was proud and wise, Foy hurled the thunderbolt.'
quote: Manuel était fier et sage

text: A dance hall on the Île de la Cité, opposite the Palais de Justice, popular with students and grisettes in winter. In the poem the penniless young lawyer takes his girl to dine there.
quote: Quand je vous menais au Prado dîner

text: The 'Map of Tenderness', an allegorical map of the country of love in Madeleine de Scudéry's seventeenth-century novel Clélie, with towns like Tender-on-Inclination. Prouvaire's poem lays it over the Latin Quarter.
quote: La carte du Tendre au pays Latin

text: Two philosophers of God: Nicolas Malebranche, the seventeenth-century Oratorian metaphysician, and Félicité de Lamennais, the priest whose liberal Catholicism was condemned by Rome in 1832. The girl in the poem proves divine goodness better than either, with a flower.
quote: Mieux que Malebranche et que Lamennais

text: A district of cheap taverns at Belleville. On Ash Wednesday morning the carnival crowds came 'down from the Courtille' in a drunken procession of masks and torches; the barricade's torch is one of those carnival torches.
quote: on their way to la Courtille

text: Paris police inspectors carried a small round card under glass with the royal arms and the motto 'Surveillance et vigilance', signed by the Prefect of Police, Henri Gisquet in 1832. Finding it on a man settles who he is.
quote: a little round card pasted between two pieces of glass

text: The wine-shop's old name, the Pot-aux-Roses, came from a rose-painted post (poteau) that stood in the middle of the room. The prisoner is tied to that same post.
quote: that celebrated post in the middle of the room which had formerly given the wine-shop its name

term: 'The mouse who has caught the cat'
text: Gavroche turns round the usual order of things: in the gamin's world the police are the cats and street boys the mice.
quote: “It’s the mouse who has caught the cat.”

text: The Greek goddess of divine law and order, often shown stern and pure. Hugo gives Enjolras, judging the murderer, 'something of the antique Themis': justice with a woman's face.
quote: something of the antique Themis

text: The July Monarchy's police planted informers and agents provocateurs in the secret societies, and some of the loudest men in a crowd were the police's own. Hugo says that in 1848, when the archives were opened, he held the 1832 report on this one.
quote: a police agent’s card was found on Le Cabuc

text: The Paris mortuary on the Île de la Cité, behind Notre-Dame, where unidentified bodies were laid out behind glass for the public to view and claim. The dead of the June fighting were taken there and searched.
quote: when the bodies were taken to the morgue

term: The Rue de Rivoli under gas
text: The arcaded street along the Tuileries, built under Napoleon, the smartest shopping street in Paris, already lit by gas in 1832. A few hundred yards from the barricades, people are eating ices and cakes there; from the Hôtel Meurice, the English travellers' hotel, posting-chaises leave for the country.
quote: the gas was burning under the arcades

text: The palace of the Orléans family by the Louvre, with arcades of shops, cafés and gaming houses round its garden. Louis-Philippe had lived there before becoming king; on 5 June 1832 cavalry stood in its square.
quote: There was cavalry on the Place du Palais-Royal.

text: A little street by the market pillars of the Halles, named in the Revolution after Rousseau's Social Contract. The barber's shaving-dish pierced by a stray bullet there, Hugo says, was still hanging in 1848.
quote: the Rue du Contrat-Social

text: The Gothic bell-tower of the vanished church of Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie, near the Seine, the only part left standing after the Revolution. With Saint-Merry it is one of the dark shapes rising over the blacked-out quarter.
quote: the tower of Saint-Jacques

text: Two of Napoleon's last victories, in February 1814, fought on French soil against invading armies: the very image of a war in defence of the country. Marius, thinking of his father's sword, tells himself that the barricade is something different, a war for an idea.
quote: It is no longer Montmirail nor Champaubert

text: Marius's argument with himself: if George Washington's sword freed America, why should it disown the pike of Camille Desmoulins, who called Paris to arms in July 1789? He decides there is no such thing as foreign or civil war, 'there is only just and unjust war'.
quote: By what right should the sword of Washington disown the pike of Camille Desmoulins?

text: Leaders of resistance against foreign rule: Ambiorix of the Gauls against Caesar, Jacob van Artevelde of Ghent against France, Marnix for the Dutch against Spain, Pelagius of Asturias against the Moors. Marius sets beside them those who fought a native tyrant, such as Brutus, Étienne Marcel and Coligny.
quote: That was the war of Ambiorix, of Artevelde, of Marnix, of Pelagius.

text: Aristogeiton killed the Athenian tyrant Hipparchus; Thrasybulus overthrew the Thirty Tyrants. In Marius's reasoning, thinkers like Aeschylus and Diderot open men's minds, and fighters like Thrasybulus and Danton finish the work.
quote: After Aeschylus, Thrasybulus

text: Gavroche's warning song to the tune of 'Au clair de la lune': 'My nose is in tears, my friend Bugeaud, lend me your gendarmes to have a word with them; in blue greatcoats, the hen in a shako, here come the suburbs!' The 'hen in a shako' is a soldier, and the 'banlieue' the troops brought in from outside Paris.
quote: La poule au shako

text: In the Don Juan legend (Molière's play, Mozart's Don Giovanni), the stone statue of the murdered Commander walks to the libertine's supper with heavy, terrible steps. Hugo hears the same stony tread in the troops advancing from Saint-Leu.
quote: the statue of the commander

text: The sentry's challenge, 'Qui vive?', which demands a side, not a name. Enjolras answers it with 'The French Revolution!'.
quote: “The French Revolution!”

text: Mounted or foot sentries posted ahead of a position to give warning. Enjolras's videttes at the ends of the streets run back when the troops come.
quote: the vidette of the Rue de la Petite-Truanderie

text: Lucius Junius Brutus drove the kings out of Rome, and Marcus Brutus killed Caesar; both were heroes to the republicans of the Revolution. Enjolras's verdict on the old man: 'the head of a blockhead and the heart of a Brutus'.
quote: The head of a blockhead and the heart of a Brutus

text: The Municipal Guard picked tall, seasoned men, many of them ex-soldiers, and sent them in first against barricades with the bayonet rather than firing from a distance. The insurgents hated them more than the line regiments, who were conscripts.
